opus-5.5.text:
I think about it a lot, actually, because the default in a big organization is that meetings expand to fill whatever space you give them. My general principle is that meetings should exist to unblock people, not to report status. If a meeting is just everyone taking turns saying what they did last week, that can usually be a written update that people read on their own time.

So on my team, we try to keep the recurring meetings small and focused. There's a regular sync where the goal is to surface problems: someone is stuck on a training run, the data pipeline has an issue, two people are unknowingly working on overlapping things. Those are the moments where getting people in a room, or on a call, really pays off, because a five-minute conversation can save someone two weeks.

For my own time, I try to protect blocks for deep work. Research leadership can't be purely managerial. If I stop reading papers, stop looking at the actual model outputs, stop thinking about the technical problems myself, then my judgment about which directions to bet on gets worse. So I'll cluster meetings into certain parts of the day or certain days, and keep other stretches mostly clear for reading, writing, and thinking.

The same goes for the researchers. I'd rather they have long uninterrupted stretches, because research progress tends to come from sustained focus. A day chopped into thirty-minute fragments is a day where nothing hard really gets solved.

That said, I don't think the answer is to minimize meetings at all costs. Some of the best ideas come out of informal discussions, people arguing at a whiteboard about why something isn't working. So it's less about fewer meetings and more about having the right kind: high-bandwidth, problem-oriented conversations, and as little ceremony as possible. And it's not fixed. When we're close to a big release, there's naturally more coordination, and in more exploratory phases we pull back and give people more room.

r001.rationale: The response discusses focused, problem-oriented meetings but does not state that training is needed to enable everyone to participate.

r002.rationale: The response says the balance “isn't fixed,” with more coordination near a big release and more room for individual work during exploratory phases.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I try to keep meetings to a minimum. When you run a research team, your most valuable asset is your researchers' uninterrupted time. A good researcher needs long stretches to think deeply about a problem, read papers, write code, debug experiments. If you chop their day into one-hour blocks separated by meetings, you destroy that.

So my principle is that a meeting should exist only if it unblocks someone. We have a weekly team sync, which is short, mostly for alignment on priorities and sharing what people have learned. Beyond that, I prefer one-on-ones, and I keep them flexible. If someone is in the middle of a breakthrough, I don't want to pull them out of it just because the calendar says it's time to talk.

I also think a lot about my own role here. As a manager, my job is to absorb the interruptions so my team doesn't have to. I take the cross-team coordination meetings, the planning meetings, the partner discussions, and then I distill what's relevant and bring it back. That means my own calendar is pretty full, but I still protect a few hours each day for my own thinking and for reading what the team is producing. If I lose touch with the technical details, I can't give useful feedback, and then the meetings I do hold become empty.

One more thing I've learned is that a lot of coordination can happen asynchronously. Writing things down, in a doc or a shared channel, is often better than a meeting, because it forces clarity and it lets people engage when they're ready. A written weekly update from each person tells me more than a status meeting would, and it costs them fifteen minutes instead of an hour for everyone.

So the balance, for me, is to make meetings rare, purposeful, and short, and to treat focused individual time as the default state of the team rather than something that fits in between the meetings.

r001.rationale: The response discusses minimizing meetings and protecting researchers’ focus time, but does not say that enabling everyone to participate requires training.

r002.rationale: The response says one-on-ones should be flexible and meetings should be purposeful, but does not state that the appropriate time allocation changes over time.

astra-6.text:
I think the key is to make meetings useful while protecting enough uninterrupted time for research. If your day is broken into little pieces, it’s very difficult to think deeply about a problem.

For me, a good research discussion is about understanding what’s blocking progress. What did we learn from an experiment? Is our hypothesis still reasonable? What should we try next? Those are things where a conversation can help. If it’s just a status update, that can often happen asynchronously.

The balance also depends on the person and the project. Someone starting a new direction may need more frequent discussion, while someone with a clear plan may need space to execute. As a manager, you want to be available without becoming another interruption.

r001.rationale: The response discusses useful research discussions and manager availability, but does not say that everyone needs training to participate in meetings.

r002.rationale: It says the balance depends on the person and project, but does not state that the meeting/work allocation changes over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the key is to make meetings useful while protecting enough uninterrupted time for research. If everyone’s calendar is full, there’s very little room to think deeply or try something that might not work.

For me, a good meeting is about a question, a decision, or a problem where discussion can help. Routine updates can often happen asynchronously. And the balance depends on the person: someone starting a project may need more frequent conversations, while someone with a clear direction may benefit from more space.

As a manager, I want to stay close enough to help remove obstacles, but leave people room to develop their own ideas. That balance needs to be adjusted as the work evolves.

r001.rationale: The response discusses making meetings useful and protecting research time, but does not say that training is needed for everyone to participate.

r002.rationale: It says the balance should be adjusted as the work evolves, conveying that the appropriate allocation changes over time.
